## Background

Steamboat Hills has a fairly long geochemistry record for a Great
Basin system -- White and coworkers characterized it geologically and
hydrologically starting in the 1950s-60s, and there's a run of gas and
water chemistry papers from the 1970s-90s: Nehring (1979, 1980) on
reservoir temperature and gas composition, Mariner and Janik (1995)
with water and gas analyses for several CPI production wells
(including well 23-5, which ends up being our main point of comparison
below), and Arehart, Coolbaugh, and Poulson (2003) arguing for a
magmatic heat source using trace elements and gas geochemistry. I've
been building a database that pulls all of this together along with
NDEP, NDWR, and our own field data, mostly for the chloride-discharge
side of the thesis -- but it also means we have a real, if sparse,
historical gas-chemistry baseline to check new samples against.

## The 2025 eruption and the fissure

In June 2025 the Lower Sinter Terrace had a geyser-like eruption that
opened a new fissure (Lindsey et al. 2026 give the fuller account of
how the activity built up over 2022-2025 before that). The well was
capped not long after, but discharge didn't stop -- it moved laterally
along the fracture system instead, and the fissure has kept
degassing/discharging since. Cary and I put together a poster on this
for GRC (Irvin and Lindsey, 2026) arguing, mostly from paired
temperature loggers and a Cl mass-balance estimate, that this looks
more like redistribution within an existing shallow conduit system
than a brand-new source turning on.

## Sampling

You, Tobias, and Karim collected three gas samples at and around the
fissure on April 29-30, 2026 -- two points right at the fissure and a
third across the road at a separate degassing spot.

| Sample | Date | Approx. location | Field temp (C) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NV26-1 | Apr 29 | at the fissure | 99.5 | co-located with a water sample we collected May 1 (see below) |
| NV26-2 | Apr 30 | fissure, second point | 96 | flagged -- possible bottle leak noted in the field, and this is also where sampling went through fresh asphalt that the gas was escaping through |
| NV26-3 | Apr 30 | across the road | 96 | second degassing area |

NV26-2 is the one I want your read on. We're not throwing it out, but
we're also not treating it the same as the other two until we hear
back on whether the leak and/or the asphalt breakthrough would
meaningfully change the result.

## What we're seeing so far

This is exploratory -- these are three samples, one of them flagged,
so I'm treating all of it as a first look rather than a result to lean
on hard.

**Air correction and geothermometry.** Surface gas is never air-free,
so before doing anything else we corrected for atmospheric
contamination (standard approach: all measured O2 treated as air,
air-derived N2 subtracted using the dry-air N2/O2 ratio, everything
renormalized). All three samples turn out to have a real amount of air
mixed in -- not surprising for shallow vent sampling instead of a
wellhead -- but NV26-2 is essentially explainable by air alone.

| Sample | Air fraction (O2-based) | D'Amore-Panichi T (C) |
|---|---|---|
| NV26-1 | 53% | 228 |
| NV26-2 | 100% | 209 (not trusted -- see above) |
| NV26-3 | 64% | 181 |

For reference, Mariner and Janik's well 23-5 T-DP values from the
1990s run 173-200 C, so NV26-1 and NV26-3 bracket that range -- and
both are well above the measured field temperatures (96-99.5 C), which
is the same pattern we're already seeing in the water geothermometers
(quartz below measured temperature, Na/K above it). It's a reasonable
result, but three samples isn't much to build on yet.

```{r fig-ratios}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
img <- gsub("\\\\", "/", file.path(normalizePath(getwd()), "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "gas_ratio_historical_comparison.png"))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img))
```

**How the two "good" samples compare to Nehring and to Mariner & Janik.**
CO2/N2, H2S/CO2, N2/Ar, and CH4/CO2 for NV26-1 and NV26-3 land closer
to Nehring's (1980) spring samples than to well 23-5 -- which makes
sense, since Nehring sampled surface springs too, not a wellhead, so a
similar degree of air mixing isn't surprising. NV26-2 sits off on its
own in every panel, again consistent with it being mostly air. Nehring
and Mariner & Janik only overlap with us on major-gas composition --
neither reports a helium isotope ratio, so that comparison stops at
CO2/H2S/N2/Ar/CH4.

**A ternary view of the same thing.** The classic way to look at this
kind of air-mixing question is an N2-He-Ar diagram (the same style
Mariner & Janik use in their own Figure 9). I plotted our three points
against well 23-5, the two usable Nehring rows, and real dry air for
reference.

```{r fig-ternary}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
#| message: false
#| warning: false
tern_path <- file.path(root, "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "gas_ternary_n2_he_ar.png")
build_gas_ternary_diagram(con, out_png = tern_path)
img2 <- gsub("\\\\", "/", normalizePath(tern_path))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img2))
```

All three of our points, and Nehring's two spring samples, cluster
right next to the air point -- well 23-5 sits noticeably further away,
toward more N2 relative to Ar and He. That lines up with the air
correction above: surface vent/spring gas looks a lot more air-like
than gas collected at a wellhead, which isn't a new idea but it's nice
to see it fall out of the data this cleanly. I used the common
He-times-100/Ar-times-10 scaling to make the plot readable, but I
haven't gone back to a primary Giggenbach reference to confirm that's
the right scaling or where the "real" air/crustal/mantle field
boundaries are supposed to sit on a plot like this -- flagged as a
question below rather than something I'm presenting as settled.

**Helium isotopes -- it turns out there's a real 1982 baseline, and it's
a surprisingly tight match.** I'd first written this saying nobody had
ever published a He-3/He-4 ratio for Steamboat -- wrong, and I'm glad
you (or whoever flagged it) caught it, because the real source turned
out to be even better than what I'd patched it with the first time.
Torgersen and Jenkins (1982, GCA) measured He isotopes in both water
and gas at four Steamboat springs. Their two gas samples they
themselves call the more reliable ones (Springs 6 and 10) both come out
at Rc/Ra = 6.0 -- our three new samples come out at 5.6-6.0. That's
about as close a match as you could ask for across 44 years, and it's a
gas-to-gas comparison specifically, which matters since their own
water-phase numbers run lower (3.9-4.5) and two of their gas values are
flagged in their own text as suspect (air mixing or the vent
contaminating itself). See the figure below. Kennedy & van Soest (2007,
Science), which is what I'd originally found this through (via Dhakal
et al.'s citation of it, not read directly at first), also names
Steamboat as a high-R/Ra Basin and Range site, but that's a regional
paper, not Steamboat-specific -- Torgersen and Jenkins is the real,
direct comparison. Arehart et al. (2003) make basically the same
magmatic-source argument from trace elements and gas geochemistry, but
cite a different, earlier Kennedy paper (2002, not the 2007 one) and
don't give a gas composition table or a He number of their own, so
they're interpretive context here rather than a number to compare
against.

```{r fig-heisotope-rup}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis
he_path <- file.path(root, "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "he_isotope_historical_comparison.png")
build_he_isotope_historical_comparison(con, out_png = he_path)
img5 <- gsub("\\\\", "/", normalizePath(he_path))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img5))
```

Panel A is the He-isotope comparison above. Panel B is the closest thing
I can show for 2026, since we don't have a dissolved-gas/He measurement
on the water side this time -- it's the gas vs. water temperature
geothermometer comparison at this same NV26-1/SBF_0001 point instead.
The pattern rhymes: in 1982 every spring's gas phase reads a higher
Rc/Ra than its own water phase, and in 2026 the gas geothermometer
reads hotter than every water method except Na/K. Different measurement
(isotope ratio vs. temperature), same qualitative story -- the gas phase
is consistently telling you something different from, and arguably
deeper/hotter than, the water at the same point, in both eras.

**One more thing worth a mention.** NV26-1 sits right on top of
SBF_0001, a water sample we collected two days later (May 1) with full
major-ion and isotope chemistry -- a mature Na-Cl thermal water
(Cl 815 mg/L). It's the first spot in the project with both phases
from essentially the same location, which matters more for the mixing
modeling described below than for anything in this section.

**Water vs. gas geothermometry, and a first real PHREEQC run.** Putting
the gas geothermometer estimate next to our existing water
geothermometers (Na/K, quartz, chalcedony -- 148 estimates across 67
real thermal samples) for the one point where we have both, NV26-1's
gas estimate (228 C) lands closest to the Na/K water estimates
(153-173 C), not the quartz/chalcedony ones (92-118 C) -- both the gas
and the Na/K signature seem to be reading a similar, deeper part of the
system than silica does.

```{r fig-geotherm-wg}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "analysis", "geothermometer_water_gas_comparison.R"))
geo_path <- file.path(root, "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "geothermometer_water_gas_comparison.png")
build_geothermometer_water_gas_figure(con, out_png = geo_path)
img3 <- gsub("\\\\", "/", normalizePath(geo_path))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img3))
```

I also went ahead and ran a real PHREEQC `GAS_PHASE` equilibration --
took SBF_0001's water chemistry and re-equilibrated it against a gas
phase seeded with NV26-1's real, air-corrected CO2:H2S ratio (96.5:3.5),
at 1 atmosphere, treated as an open system (i.e. assuming the fissure
keeps resupplying gas rather than it being a small fixed pocket).

```{r fig-gasphase-rup}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis
gp_path <- file.path(root, "output", "figures", "gas_analysis", "gas_phase_fischer_pairing_before_after.png")
img4 <- gsub("\\\\", "/", normalizePath(gp_path))
knitr::asis_output(sprintf("![](%s)", img4))
```

The result: pH drops from the water's measured 8.3 down to a modeled
6.3, and calcite/aragonite/dolomite all flip from supersaturated to
undersaturated. My read is that this means the water as sampled isn't
actually sitting in equilibrium with the gas as sampled -- which could
mean they're not really the same fluid parcel, that gas and liquid
separate out before either one reaches the surface, or that the real
reservoir pressure (not the 1 atm I used, which was a simplification)
changes things. I don't have the background to know which of those is
most likely, which is part of why I'm asking below.

## How this fits into the rest of the thesis

The short version is that this is the first real gas dataset the
project has, and it slots into a few places we'd already scoped out
but had no real data for:

- The D'Amore-Panichi geothermometer work above reuses code that had
  only ever been run against your group's own historical numbers
  (Mariner & Janik) as a check -- this is the first time it's been run
  on a Steamboat sample we actually collected.
- We'd had a PHREEQC gas-phase/mixing setup built for a while, waiting on
  a real dissolved-gas sample to test it against -- NV26-1 is the first
  one, and the real run above is already a result, not just a
  capability anymore.
- The NV26-1/SBF_0001 pairing is a natural input to the mixing-model
  chapter -- a real gas end-member next to a real water end-member from
  (almost) the same spot and the same week.
- More broadly, it's a second, independent way to ask whether the
  system has cooled/diluted the way the water geochemistry suggests,
  which matters for the "redistribution vs. new source" question the
  poster raised.

## Questions for you

Mostly I want to make sure we're using and describing your group's
work correctly before any of this goes further:

- How should we cite the gas analyses in the thesis, and separately if
  this turns into a conference abstract or paper -- Fischer's lab and
  Barry's lab specifically, or is there a preferred citation you'd
  want us to use?
- Is the air correction above a reasonable way to handle Giggenbach
  bottle samples collected this way, or does your group normally do
  something different that we should match?
- On the PHREEQC gas-phase run -- is 1 atm/open-system a reasonable
  starting assumption for this, or is there a better estimate of the
  real pressure/volume this gas phase should represent at depth? And is
  the disequilibrium result (pH/carbonate SI shifting a lot) actually
  surprising, or is that just what you'd expect for a water and gas
  sampled two days and some distance apart rather than from the exact
  same parcel?
- On the ternary plot -- is the He-times-100/Ar-times-10 scaling I used
  the right convention, and is there a reference version of that
  diagram (with real air/crustal/mantle field boundaries) I should be
  plotting these points against instead of just showing them relative
  to a single air point?
- On NV26-2 -- is the leak serious enough that the sample shouldn't be
  used at all, or is it still usable with the caveat we've got on it?
- Should we hold off on presenting any interpretation of the noble gas
  / carbon isotope numbers until you, Tobias, or Karim have had a
  chance to look at them, or is what's here reasonable to go forward
  with as a preliminary read?
- Would you, Tobias, and/or Karim want to be coauthors if this turns
  into a conference abstract or paper down the line?
